studies.Reference: An Assessment of Serum Selenium Concentration in Women with Ovarian Cancer.
studies.Authors: Kluza M, Paszek S, Kluza K, Januszek S, Potocka N, Skrzypa M, Zuchowska A, Wróbel A, Baszuk P, Marciniak W, Misiek M, Lubiński J, Gronwald J, Zawlik I, Kluz T
studies.comparison_type: Low vs High selenium (multivariable) [inverted ⇒ high vs low]
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: The measurements of selenium in the collected blood samples were performed using an ICP mass spectrometer.

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: 314 women (157 diseased patients and 157 healthy ones) matched in terms of age and BMI were included in the study.
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: In univariable and multivariable analyzes, a clear relationship between low selenium concentration and the occurrence of ovarian cancer was found (35.3 (95% CI: 11.2-111; p < 0.001) and 45.8 (95% CI: 12.8-164; p < 0.001)).
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: A clear relationship between low selenium concentration and the occurrence of ovarian cancer was found
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: serum selenium levels; The mean concentration of selenium was lower among diseased ones than among controls (53.31 μg/L vs. 78.99 μg/L).

studies.Reference: Supplemental Selenium May Decrease Ovarian Cancer Risk in African-American Women.
studies.Authors: Terry PD, Qin B, Camacho F, Moorman PG, Alberg AJ, Barnholtz-Sloan JS, Bondy M, Cote ML, Funkhouser E, Guertin KA, Peters ES, Schwartz AG, Schildkraut JM, Bandera EV
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Women with the highest intakes of supplemental selenium (>20 μg/d) had an ∼30% lower risk of ovarian cancer than those with no supplemental intake

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: 406 ovarian cancer cases and 632 age- and site-matched controls of African-American descent recruited from AACES
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: Women with the highest intakes of supplemental selenium (>20 μg/d) had an ∼30% lower risk of ovarian cancer than those with no supplemental intake (OR: 0.67; 95% CI: 0.46, 0.97)
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: Women with the highest intakes of supplemental selenium (>20 μg/d) had an ∼30% lower risk of ovarian cancer

studies.Reference: Total and individual antioxidant intake and risk of epithelial ovarian cancer.
studies.Authors: Gifkins D, Olson SH, Paddock L, King M, Demissie K, Lu SE, Kong AN, Rodriguez-Rodriguez L, Bandera EV
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Dietary intake was ascertained using the Block food frequency questionnaire (FFQ)

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: A total of 205 ovarian cancer cases and 390 controls were included.
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: We found a strong inverse association with selenium from food sources (OR: 0.41; 95 % CI: 0.20-0.85, for the highest vs. lowest tertile of dietary selenium intake).
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: We found a strong inverse association with selenium from food sources
extraction_supporting_text.outcome_definition: Cases were women ages 21 years and older with newly diagnosed epithelial ovarian cancer who resided in six counties of New Jersey.
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: selenium from food sources... for the highest vs. lowest tertile of dietary selenium intake

headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger's test indicates no significant funnel plot asymmetry (p=0.2282). The distribution of studies appears symmetric, suggesting a lower risk of publication bias.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 3 studies yielded an overall effect size of 0.23 (95% CI: 0.06–0.93), suggesting that selenium is associated with a lower risk of ovarian cancer. However, this association should be interpreted with caution, as there was very high between-study heterogeneity (I² = 92.03%), reflecting highly inconsistent results across studies.
